summary: Defines DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM), which lets a signing domain take responsibility for an email message using public-key cryptography and keys published in the DNS. Receivers can check the signature to verify the source and contents. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 6376.

plainLanguage.summary: DKIM lets a domain put its mark on the email it sends. The sending server computes a fingerprint of the message, signs it with a private key, and puts the result in a new header. A receiver fetches the matching public key from the sending domain's DNS records, recomputes the fingerprint, and checks the two agree. A forged message will not match.

questions: how to verify an email signature
where is the dkim public key stored
subtitle: Signing an email message so a receiver can confirm the sending domain really sent it.

tldr.problem: A mail message carries a From address that anyone can type, so a receiver has no way to tell a genuine message from a forged one, nor to notice that the text was altered on the way.
tldr.mechanism: The sending domain signs a hash of the message with a private key and adds a DKIM-Signature header field. The receiver looks the public key up in the sending domain's own DNS, recomputes the hash, and checks the signature against it.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4871 is a Proposed Standard from May 2007 and has been obsoleted by RFC 6376, which restates the DKIM signature specification. The RFC also notes that RFC 5672 updates it.

today: RFC 4871 is a Proposed Standard from May 2007, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 6376, which restates the DKIM signature specification; the unit metadata also lists RFC 5672 as updating it. The RFC itself notes that it obsoletes RFC 4870 and that DKIM is designed to be extensible to other key fetching services as they become available.

sections.title: Why DKIM Exists
sections.content:
DKIM defines a mechanism by which mail messages can be cryptographically signed, so that a signing domain can claim responsibility for introducing a message into the mail stream. A recipient verifies the signature by querying the signer's domain directly for the public key, and can then confirm that the message was attested to by a party holding the private key for that domain.

The RFC sets out where DKIM differs from earlier ways of signing mail, such as S/MIME and OpenPGP. The signature goes in a message header field, so neither people nor existing mail software is confused by signature content in the body. There is no dependency on certificate authorities, and no dependency on any new protocol or service for key distribution or revocation. A failed signature does not force the message to be rejected. Encryption is not attempted at all, and archiving is not a design goal.

Two more design points follow from that. DKIM separates the identity of the signer from the claimed author of the message, so a receiver can decide what to do with a message based on who signed it. And it needs no certificate infrastructure: the verifier asks the claimed signer's DNS entry for the public key rather than a third party, which means DKIM currently depends on DNS administration and on the security of the DNS.
sections.plainLanguage: The problem with email is that the From line is just text. DKIM adds a way for a sending organisation to prove it really sent a message, without asking any third party to vouch for it and without changing how mail travels.

sections.title: The DKIM-Signature Header Field
sections.content:
The signature travels in a header field called DKIM-Signature, whose value is a list of tag and value pairs. Unrecognised tags must be ignored, tags must be read case-sensitively, and a tag with an empty value is not the same as an omitted tag. A tag that appears twice makes the whole list invalid.

The required tags are the version v=, which must have the value 1; the algorithm a=, naming the hash and signature algorithms; the signature b= itself, in base64; the body hash bh=, also base64; the signing domain d=; the list of signed header fields h=; and the selector s=. Optional tags carry the canonicalization algorithms c=, the signing identity i=, the hashed body length l=, the key query method q=, the signature timestamp t= and the expiration x=.

The field being created or verified is itself part of the signature calculation, placed after the other signed header fields, with its own b= value treated as empty while the hash is computed. The RFC recommends treating the field like a trace header, so it should be prepended to the message and not reordered.
sections.plainLanguage: One new header holds the whole signature, written as a list of labelled values. The labelled values tell the reader which algorithm was used, which domain signed, which header fields were covered, what the message body hashed to, and the signature itself.

sections.title: Finding the Public Key
sections.content:
Because a domain may have more than one key at a time, the key namespace is divided by selectors. A selector might name an office, a date, or an individual user. The RFC gives three reasons selectors are needed: to delegate signing for one address for a period to a partner, to let frequent travellers send mail locally without connecting to a particular submission agent, and to serve affinity domains that forward mail but do not run a submission agent.

Selectors also make it possible to replace keys on a routine basis. A domain that moves from the selector january2005 to february2005 advertises both public keys for the transition period, then removes the old one. Reusing a selector with a new key is discouraged, because it makes a message that failed because the key expired indistinguishable from a forged message.

Keys are stored in DNS TXT records, in a subdomain named _domainkey. For a signature with the domain example.com and the selector foo.bar, the query is for foo.bar._domainkey.example.com. The record holds a tag list of its own, with a version tag that must read DKIM1, the key material in a p= tag, and an optional granularity tag g= that restricts the key to a particular local part. An empty p= means the key has been revoked. The RFC notes that a large key may not fit in a 512-byte DNS response packet, and that keys must be at least 1024 bits for long-lived use, while verifiers must handle keys from 512 to 2048 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: The public key is published in the DNS of the signing domain, in a record named after a selector. The selector lets one domain run several keys at once and swap them over without breaking mail that is still in flight.

sections.title: Canonicalization and the Message Hashes
sections.content:
Some mail servers and relays change messages in transit, which would otherwise break a signature. DKIM deals with this by canonicalizing the message before hashing it, so that harmless changes do not alter the result. Two header algorithms are defined, simple and relaxed, and two body algorithms with the same names. The choice is recorded in the c= tag, and it does not affect the message that is actually sent.

Two hashes are computed. The first covers the canonicalized body, truncated to the length given by the l= tag if there is one, and its base64 form goes into the bh= tag. The second covers the selected header fields, including the DKIM-Signature field itself with an empty signature value, and it is this hash that is signed. Anything after the body length given by l= is not covered by the signature at all, which the RFC flags as an attack surface in its security section.

The RFC recommends that signers include the From field in every signature, along with headers such as Subject, Date, Message-ID and the MIME headers, and not include Return-Path, Received, Bcc or DKIM-Signature. It also advises against using l= unless the signer expects an intermediate processor to append text, and against a body length of zero.
sections.plainLanguage: Two hashes are computed, one over the body and one over the chosen header fields, and the second one is what gets signed. Before hashing, the message is put into a standard form so that a relay adding a space or refolding a line does not break the signature.

sections.title: Signer Actions and Verifier Actions
sections.content:
The signer picks a key and selector, normalizes the message so that transport will not alter the parts being signed, chooses the header fields to sign, computes the two hashes, signs the header hash with the private key, and inserts the resulting DKIM-Signature header field before any other DKIM-Signature fields. An agent that modifies a message on the way, such as a mailing list manager adding unsubscribe text, should check any existing signature first and make its changes before re-signing.

The verifier takes the signature header fields from the message and, for each one, validates its format, fetches the public key, and recomputes the hashes. A missing key record is a permanent failure; a key query that does not answer may be a temporary failure, and the verifier may hold the message for later or try another signature. A malformed key record, a key whose granularity does not match the signing identity, an empty key data field meaning the key has been revoked, and a body hash that does not match are all permanent failures.

The RFC notes that verifiers should not treat a message with bad signatures and no good signature differently from a message with no signature at all, because that is local policy. It also warns that an attacker could send a message with a large number of faulty signatures, each of which costs a DNS lookup and some CPU, so verifiers may limit how many signatures they attempt.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing is a matter of hashing the chosen parts of the message and encrypting that hash with the private key. Checking is the same work done with the public key, plus a lookup to fetch it. Both sides are given step by step, including what to do when a key is missing, revoked or malformed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC opens by noting that any mechanism aimed at stemming the flow of spam is subject to intensive attack. It then works through the ways DKIM can be abused.

The body length tag is the first problem. If the limit does not cover the closing part of a multipart message, an attacker who intercepts a properly signed message can append a new body part. Some receiving programs keep displaying after a closing HTML tag, so appended content can be laid over the original text. A second problem is a misappropriated private key: if the key for a user sits on their computer and is not well protected, malware can send mail as that user. The RFC's answer is that DKIM is only intended as a sufficient method of proving authenticity, not strong cryptographic proof of authorship, and that other technologies address that.

On the DNS side, widespread use of DKIM means many more queries to the claimed signing domain, and a verifier can be prompted to fetch a key record of an attacker's choosing through a name chaining attack. The RFC recommends that the name servers used enforce strict checking of glue and other information in DNS responses. Finally, the section on replay attacks describes a spammer who has a message signed by a legitimate server and then resends the unmodified signed copy to many recipients, and notes that large verifiers might spot unusually large volumes of mail with the same signature in a short period.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC is careful about the ways the scheme can be turned against a receiver. A body length that stops too early lets an attacker append content, a stolen private key lets malware send as the owner, and a replayed signed message looks perfectly valid to the receiver.

viz.caption: THE TAGS OF THE DKIM-Signature HEADER FIELD (RFC 4871)

items.label: Version
items.desc: Must be included and must have the value 1. Verifiers compare it as a string.

items.label: Signing algorithm
items.desc: Required. Verifiers must support rsa-sha1 and rsa-sha256; signers should sign using rsa-sha256.

items.label: Signature
items.desc: Required. The base64 signature over the header hash. Whitespace in the value is ignored.

items.label: Body hash
items.desc: Required. The base64 hash of the canonicalized message body.

items.label: Canonicalization
items.desc: Optional, default simple/simple. Names the header and body canonicalization algorithms.

items.label: Signing domain
items.desc: Required. The domain that will be queried for the public key.

items.label: Signed header fields
items.desc: Required. The colon-separated list of header field names that were signed, in the order presented.

items.label: Signing identity
items.desc: Optional. The identity on whose behalf the message was signed. Its domain part must be the same as or a subdomain of d=.

items.label: Body length
items.desc: Optional. The number of octets of the canonicalized body that were hashed. Anything beyond it is not covered.

items.label: Query method
items.desc: Optional, default dns/txt. The colon-separated list of methods used to retrieve the public key.

items.label: Selector
items.desc: Required. The selector that subdivides the key namespace of the signing domain.

items.label: Signature timestamp
items.desc: Optional. Seconds since January 1, 1970 in UTC, when the signature was created.

items.label: Expiration
items.desc: Optional. The absolute date and time after which the signature may be treated as invalid.

viz.caption: HOW DKIM DIFFERS FROM EARLIER SIGNING SCHEMES (RFC 4871)

items.title: Signature in a header
items.text: Neither human recipients nor existing mail software is confused by signature content in the message body.

items.title: No certificate authority
items.text: The verifier asks the signer's own DNS for the public key.

items.title: No new protocol
items.text: No new service is needed for key distribution or revocation.

items.title: Failure does not reject
items.text: A signature that fails to verify does not force the message to be refused.

items.title: No encryption
items.text: DKIM signs messages; it does not encrypt them.
